Zcash needs a dovish Fed or a US-Iran breakthrough to reverse the bearish trend
body: Zcash has come under significant selling pressure over the past few days as the broader crypto selloff, driven by hawkish Fed repricing and US-Iran tensions, weighed on risk sentiment.

The main culprit was Fed Governor Waller's very hawkish speech, in which he floated the possibility of a larger 50 bps hike at the December meeting. His remarks triggered a quick hawkish repricing, which was then exacerbated by the higher than expected US CPI data.
Moreover, Trump's statement that the US doesn't need a deal with Iran triggered a rally in oil prices, adding to concerns about inflation and tighter monetary policy.

Looking ahead, Zcash will likely remain under pressure as long as the negative macro backdrop persists. We will probably need a more dovish Fed or a US-Iran breakthrough to change the risk sentiment and trigger a rebound in Zcash.

On the daily chart, we can see that Zcash bounced near the major upward trendline after a big selloff. If we get another drop into the trendline, we can expect the buyers to step in there, with a defined risk blow the trendline, to position for a rally into the major downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into the 500 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting a break below the major upward trendline. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to pile in for a correction into the major downward trendline.

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the sellers will have a better risk to reward setup around the trendline, while the buyers will need a breakout to open the door for new highs. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

Today we have Fed Chair Warsh speaking. Tomorrow, we get the US Retail Sales. On Wednesday, we have the FOMC meeting minutes. On Thursday, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. The focus will remain on Fed speakers and the US-Iran developments.

news.title: Crude oil remains supported amid the prolonged US-Iran standoff and risks of military escalation
body: Crude oil has been bottoming out near the 87.00 handle as the market realised that the US-Iran standoff may drag on longer than expected, with the additional risk that Trump decides to pursue another military campaign.

As a reminder, the culprit for the increase in prices was Trump’s post on Truth Social stating that the US doesn’t need a deal with Iran. Moreover, Trump warned that the US would not hesitate to take further military action if current measures fail to achieve objectives.
According to Axios, the USS Roosevelt has arrived in the Middle East with the aircraft carrier joining two others operating in the CENTCOM area.

Meanwhile, Iran targeted a military base in Bahrain with six drones, marking its first direct strike on the country in several weeks. Moreover, Iran reported multiple tanker incidents involving naval mines in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the past 48 hours, warning oil companies that parts of the southern shipping route remain mined and that vessels cooperating with US forces risk coming under fire.
Finally, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson ruled out suspending uranium enrichment activities or reducing enrichment levels.

It goes without saying that a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations would trigger a significant selloff and take oil prices back to pre-war levels relatively quickly. But as of now, this scenario looks much less probable.

An escalation or a prolonged stalemate should keep oil prices supported, although there’s also a chance that Trump decides to proceed with limited strikes against Iran’s nuclear facilities before exiting the war.

On the daily chart, we can see that crude oil (CFD contract) is basically bottoming out near the key 87.00 handle amid heightened US-Iran tensions. We can expect the buyers to continue to step in around these levels, with a defined risk below the 87.00 level, to keep targeting the 110.00 resistance. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking below the 87.00 level to start positioning for a drop into the 80.00 handle next.

On the 4 hour chart, we now have an upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the buyers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into the 110.00 resistance, with the 92.50 level as the first target. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to pile in for a drop into the 80.00 handle next.

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the buyers will have a better risk to reward setup around the upward trendline, while the sellers will need a break below it to open the door for new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

Today we have Fed Chair Warsh speaking. Tomorrow, we get the US Retail Sales. On Wednesday, we have the FOMC meeting minutes. On Thursday, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. The focus will remain on US-Iran developments.

news.title: Hawkish Fed repricing and Iran tensions trigger a major Bitcoin liquidation wave
body: Bitcoin faced a big wave of liquidations over the past few days as the hawkish Fed repricing tightened financial conditions, weighing on the crypto market.
The culprit was of course the very hawkish Fed’s Waller speech in which he also floated the idea of a larger 50 bps hike at the December meeting.
His remarks triggered a strong hawkish repricing which was then exacerbated by the hotter than expected US CPI data.
Moreover, Trump stated on Truth Social that the US doesn’t need a deal with Iran, triggering a rally in oil prices and weighing further on the risk sentiment.
Looking ahead, Bitcoin will likely remain under pressure amid the negative macro backdrop. We will likely need a more dovish Fed or a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations to reverse the trend.

On the daily chart, we can see that Bitcoin erased all the gains since August after the more hawkish Fed stance and the hotter than expected US CPI data. The price bounced from the 62,000 support amid some profit-taking, but the macro backdrop remains negative. If we get a pullback into the 67,000 resistance, we can expect the sellers to step in, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting the 58,000 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the major downward trendline around the 75,000 level.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback into the trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next.

On the 1 hour chart, we have some consolidation after the strong selloff. We have a swing low around the 63,750 level that could act as support. The buyers will likely step in there, with a defined risk below the level, to position for a pullback into the 67,000 resistance. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to pile in for a drop into the 62,000 support, targeting a break below it. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

Today we have Fed Chair Warsh speaking. Tomorrow, we get the US Retail Sales. On Wednesday, we have the FOMC meeting minutes. On Thursday, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. The focus will remain on Fed speakers and the US-Iran stalemate.

news.title: Gold threatens a major breakdown amid a more hawkish Fed. What to watch next?
body: Gold continues to remain under pressure amid a more hawkish Fed stance. As a reminder, the precious metal erased all the gains since the start of November after Fed’s Waller delivered a very hawkish speech in which he also floated the idea of a larger 50 bps hike at the December meeting.

His remarks triggered a strong hawkish repricing which was then exacerbated by the hotter than expected US CPI data. Moreover, Trump stated on Truth Social that the US doesn’t need a deal with Iran, triggering a rally in oil prices and the US dollar.

Looking ahead, I would expect rate hikes to start putting significant downward pressure on the stock market and long-term Treasury yields amid increased growth concerns given the longer than expected US-Iran tensions.

I think that in the current context, if Trump decides to escalate things with Iran, inflation expectations would rise alongside a weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment. And this should ultimately be bullish for gold. At the same time, if we get a de-escalation, we could see a dovish repricing on easing inflation concerns, which should also support gold in the short-term.
There are certainly strong headwinds for gold at the moment, so these fundamental views will need to be paired with technicals for a confirmation of a change in momentum.

On the daily chart, we can see that gold (CFD contract) is trading below the key support zone around the 3,885 level and the major upward trendline. We can expect the sellers to continue to step in around these levels, with a defined risk above the broken trendline, to extend the drop into the 3,500 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price rising back above the broken trendline to start piling in for a rally into the 4,700 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to pile in for a rally into the 4,700 level, with the 4,150 level as the first target.

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the sellers will have a better risk to reward setup around the downward trendline, while the buyers will need a break above it to open the door for new highs. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

news.title: Goldman sees Brent at $78 by end-2027 as oil surplus returns, flags near-term upside risk
body: Goldman’s path implies Brent averaging nearly $8 below current levels next year, and about $18 lower by end-2027. That gives oil bears a solid medium-term anchor. In the near term, though, the market is still driven by the war. Confirmation of the IRGC’s tanker-sinking claims could quickly rebuild the risk premium that Goldman expects to fade. Monday’s dip suggests traders are leaning toward the surplus story for now. The diesel forecast matters for inflation. At $150 a barrel, products stay costly even as crude eases, so energy keeps feeding into the inflation concerns Fed officials raised over the weekend.
Goldman’s message on oil is patience: a surplus is coming and prices should fall, but until the Gulf calms down, the risks over the next few weeks still point upward.

Goldman Sachs expects oil prices to drift lower over the next year as the market returns to surplus. It forecasts Brent crude to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and ease to $78 by December 2027, though it warned of upside risks in the near term from attacks on shipping in the Middle East, Reuters reported.

For US crude, the bank sees West Texas Intermediate averaging $78 a barrel next year and slipping to $70 by the end of 2027. Refined products should also ease but stay well above historical norms, with US wholesale diesel forecast to average $150 a barrel in 2027.

The core of the call is supply. In Goldman’s base case, oil production will exceed end-use demand by 2 million barrels per day in 2027. That surplus is large enough to pull prices down from current levels, even if some war-related risk premium lingers.

The bank was careful to present the risks as running in both directions. In the near term, it said prices could rise if attacks on shipping intensify, if oil infrastructure is damaged or if the risk premium rebuilds. Over the medium term, the risk is to the downside, through stronger supply, weaker demand or a smaller risk premium than it assumes.

That near-term risk is real. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed over the weekend that two tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and that one of them, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels, sank. There has been no independent confirmation.

Even so, prices fell on Monday on expectations of a supply surplus. Shipments through Hormuz were reported to be close to pre-war levels, and Washington eased domestic fuel movements by extending its Jones Act waiver. Brent was trading around $95.50 earlier in Asia, well above Goldman’s 2027 average, which implies significant downside if the bank’s surplus view plays out.
The gap between today’s prices and the forecast path leaves the oil market hinging on one question: whether supply disruption in the Gulf fades or flares up again.

news.title: Japan economy shrinks 0.1% in Q3, first fall in 4 quarters as inflation hits households
body: The pushback from economists matters more for markets than the headline miss. If weak consumption is read as a sign of inflation rather than a reason to pause, December hike pricing should hold. That limits any lasting yen weakness from the data, although USD/JPY near 160 remains in intervention territory. The risk lies in the board split some economists flagged. Further soft consumption data could give the doves more influence and push hike timing back, which would weigh on the yen and lift JGBs. Oil is the link in the middle. Energy-driven inflation is both hurting households and pushing the BOJ to tighten, so higher crude makes the policy dilemma worse.
Japan’s shoppers are buckling under inflation, but rather than giving the BOJ a reason to pause, the squeeze on households is being read as further proof that rates need to keep rising.

Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter as rising living costs forced households to cut back on spending. Economists say the weakness is unlikely to knock the Bank of Japan off its tightening path, Reuters reported.

Gross domestic product fell an annualised 0.1%, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth, following an upwardly revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. It was the first contraction in four quarters. On a quarterly basis, output slipped 0.02%, versus expectations of a 0.1% rise.

Households did most of the damage. Private consumption, which makes up more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, slightly worse than the expected 0.2% drop. Persistent inflation, heavy rain and typhoons weighed on spending. Purchases of cars and air conditioners also fell back after a temporary boost from tax and regulatory changes in the prior quarter. Economists warned that higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will keep squeezing households’ purchasing power, even as wages rise.

Trade also took away from growth. Net external demand cut 0.6 percentage point, more than the expected 0.4 point drag. Imports jumped as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified its supply following disruption from the war in the Middle East.
Business investment was the bright spot. It rose 1.6% against a 1.5% forecast, supported by spending on labour-saving technology and AI-related projects.

Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said better employment and income conditions, along with policy measures, should support a gradual recovery, but stressed the need to monitor the Middle East situation closely.

For the BOJ, which raised rates in June and September, economists say the miss changes little. Several argued that weak consumption is itself a symptom of high prices, which strengthens the case for further hikes, and many expect the next move as soon as December. One note cautioned, however, that if consumer weakness persists, it could widen divisions on the board and give more dovish members grounds to argue for caution.
That debate gets an early test later on Monday, when hawkish board member Hajime Takata speaks at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday).

news.title: Gold slips toward $3,876 ahead of Warsh as Fed speakers line up behind tighter policy
body: How the market reacts to Warsh will depend on tone more than detail. If he gives weight to AI as a future disinflationary force, traders could read it as a reason the Fed can stop after a few more hikes. That would offer relief to front-end Treasury yields and to gold. If he echoes Schmid’s view that AI demand responds to rates, it backs a longer tightening cycle and supports the US dollar. Gold remains the most exposed asset. With ETF selling risk now flagged and $4,000 broken, a hawkish lean could extend losses quickly. For equities, his comments on AI land the day before Nvidia’s results and will feed straight into how investors value the AI trade.

-- Warsh has staked part of his Fed leadership on the idea that AI can ease inflation, and on Monday he makes that case to a room of colleagues who have spent the past few days warning it is doing the opposite.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh gives opening remarks at the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference on Monday at 17:00 GMT (12:00 pm ET), hosted by the San Francisco Fed. The appearance follows a run of hawkish commentary from his colleagues over the past few days, and a December rate increase is widely expected.

The forum will bring together technology executives, economists and employers to examine whether artificial intelligence will lower inflation, push prices higher or displace workers. It is the first major public event for one of five task forces Warsh set up after taking office in May. He flagged it in October, when he described the surge in AI investment as one of the factors behind higher inflation. Warsh has argued that AI could eventually help firms produce more at lower cost and ease price pressure. Some colleagues see the AI boom adding to inflation today, with the productivity gains still unproven.

That debate has been front and centre in recent days. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said inflation is uncomfortably above target and heading the wrong way, and rejected the idea that AI-driven demand is beyond the reach of higher rates. Boston Fed President Susan Collins backed a steady, gradual pace of hikes, but said the eventual rate path may end up higher than she had expected. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the trajectory of inflation is the most important signal for policy, and warned that higher energy prices risk a broader rise, with PCE inflation at 3.6% in September.
The Fed raised rates to a 3.75% to 4.00% range in September and held in October. Markets are fully priced for a quarter-point increase on December 8-9, with a small chance of a larger move.

Gold has taken the brunt of that hawkish shift. The metal slipped in Asian trade to around $3,876 an ounce, extending a slide of almost 7% since last Tuesday, after Goldman Sachs cut its end-2027 forecast to $4,650 from $4,800 on expectations of a further hike in March 2027.

Opening remarks at a themed conference may carry little direct policy guidance, and Warsh said in October that he does not prejudge meetings. Any comment on AI’s effect on inflation, however, will be read for clues about December. Fed minutes follow on Wednesday at 19:00 GMT.
